1

Reading · technology in everyday life

1.1 Discuss. Which app on your phone have you been using most this month? Which one could you delete tomorrow without noticing?

KEY WORDS

a feature something an app or device can do

intuitive easy to use without instructions

clutter too many things, badly organised

back up to save a second copy

What's Your Favourite App?

I've been asking people this question for a month now, and the answers have surprised me. Almost nobody names the apps they use most. They name the apps they like most — and those turn out to be two very different lists.

Dilnoza, a nurse, has been using a hospital scheduling app every day for three years. She has never once enjoyed it. Her favourite, she says, is a small note-taking app she opens perhaps twice a week: “It has almost no features, and that's exactly why I like it. Everything else on my phone has been getting more complicated for years. That one hasn't changed since I installed it.”

That comment turns out to be common. When people describe an app they love, they rarely mention power; they mention calm. The most-loved apps do one thing, do it quickly, and then get out of the way. The most-used apps, by contrast, are usually the ones designed to keep you inside them — which is precisely why we use them, and precisely why we resent them.

Developers have understood this for a while, and some have started removing features rather than adding them. It is a harder sell than it sounds: a longer feature list looks better in an advertisement, and the people who choose software for a company are rarely the people who have to use it all day. Still, the direction of travel seems clear. After twenty years of collecting clutter, we have been slowly learning that less can be a feature too.

2

Grammar · present perfect simple and continuous

PRESENTATION

PRESENT PERFECT SIMPLE — the result, how many, how much, finished:

I've written three emails. · She has read the whole report.

PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS — the activity, how long, still going or just stopped:

I've been writing emails all morning. · She has been reading for hours.

Simple — the result

Continuous — the activity

How many have you sent?

How long have you been working?

I've fixed the problem.

I've been fixing it all day.

He's learnt 200 words.

He's been learning Chinese for a year.

She's made three calls.

She's been making calls since nine.

ERROR WARNING

State verbs have no continuous form:

I've been knowing him for years. ✗ I've known him for years. ✓

Use the simple when you say how many; the continuous when you say how long:

I've been writing three emails. ✗ I've written three emails. ✓

Everyday English · making and responding to suggestions

4.1 Read the conversation.

Kamola My laptop has been freezing every ten minutes. I've tried everything.

Rustam Why don't you check how much storage you've got left?

Kamola That's a good idea, actually. It is quite full.

Rustam You could also delete the programs you never open.

Kamola Hmm, I'm not sure. I might need them one day.

Rustam How about moving them to an external drive instead?

Kamola Now that I like. I'll do it this evening.
